topic: Chemistry — Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock
subject: combined-science

items.q: Crude oil is found in rocks. What was crude oil formed from?
items.correct: The remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton
items.misconception: The remains of dinosaurs and other large animals buried in mud
items.why: Crude oil is called a fossil fuel, and dinosaurs are the fossils children meet first, so the two ideas become attached to one another. The specification is precise: the biomass was mainly plankton, tiny marine organisms. Large animals contributed effectively nothing to crude oil.
items.random_wrong: The remains of ancient forests of land plants buried in swamp

items.q: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?
items.correct: New crude oil forms far more slowly than we use it up
items.misconception: New oil is forming at the same rate that we use it
items.why: Students hear that oil is still being made and conclude that supply is being topped up at a useful rate. Formation takes millions of years. Compared with the rate at which we extract it, the rate of formation is effectively zero, so the resource is finite.
items.random_wrong: It is only found in a small number of countries on Earth

items.q: What is a hydrocarbon?
items.correct: A molecule made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only
items.misconception: A molecule made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms
items.why: Most familiar organic molecules met later – alcohols, sugars, carboxylic acids – do contain oxygen, so oxygen feels like part of the package. The word 'only' is doing the work. As soon as a third element such as oxygen is present the molecule is not a hydrocarbon.
items.random_wrong: Any compound that contains carbon in its molecules

items.q: Which statement about crude oil is correct?
items.correct: It is a mixture of a great many compounds
items.misconception: It is one compound with a single fixed formula
items.why: It arrives as one black liquid with one name, and named substances in chemistry usually have one formula. Crude oil is a mixture: its compounds are not chemically joined, which is exactly why they can be separated by fractional distillation.
items.random_wrong: It is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only

items.q: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes?
items.correct: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbons, plus two
items.misconception: CₙH₂ₙ — exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons
items.why: CₙH₂ₙ is the tidier pattern and is the formula of the alkenes, which is met alongside it, so the two get swapped. Alkanes are saturated and carry two extra hydrogen atoms at the ends of the chain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. CₙH₂ₙ belongs to the alkenes.
items.random_wrong: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — twice as many hydrogens as carbon, less two

items.q: An alkane molecule contains 7 carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?
items.correct: C₇H₁₆, using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
items.misconception: C₇H₁₅, from CₙH₂ₙ₊₁
items.why: The '+2' is remembered as 'a small number added on' without recalling which, so ±1 and −2 look equally reasonable. Check against a known member: methane has one carbon and four hydrogens, and 2 × 1 + 2 = 4. Only +2 works.
items.random_wrong: C₇H₉, since 7 + 2 = 9

items.q: What are the first four members of the alkanes, in order?
items.correct: Methane, ethane, propane, butane
items.misconception: Methane, ethene, propene and butene
items.why: The prefixes are shared between the two families, so only the -ane/-ene ending distinguishes them and it is easily lost. The ending carries the family: -ane means alkane, -ene means alkene. The first four alkanes all end in -ane.
items.random_wrong: Methane, ethane, propane, pentane

items.q: An alkane can be shown as a molecular formula or as a displayed formula. What extra information does the displayed formula give?
items.correct: It shows the bonds between the atoms
items.misconception: It shows how many atoms there are of each
items.why: Both representations show the same atoms, so the atom count is the feature that stands out; the lines are treated as decoration. The atom count is exactly what the molecular formula already gives. The extra information in a displayed formula is the bonding – which atom is joined to which.
items.random_wrong: It shows the charge on each of the atoms

items.q: Ethane has the molecular formula C₂H₆. How many covalent bonds are shown in its displayed formula?
items.correct: Seven, one C–C bond plus six C–H bonds
items.misconception: Eight, a C=C bond plus six C–H bonds
items.why: Two carbon atoms next to each other suggests a double bond, especially once alkenes have been drawn. Ethane is an alkane and is saturated: every bond is single. C₂H₆ has seven single bonds in total.
items.random_wrong: Six, just the six C–H bonds are drawn

items.q: Which of these substances is an alkane?
items.correct: C₅H₁₂ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 + 2
items.misconception: C₅H₁₀ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 exactly
items.why: CₙH₂ₙ is the tidier pattern and is the formula of the alkenes, which is met alongside it, so the two get swapped. Alkanes are saturated and carry two extra hydrogen atoms at the ends of the chain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. CₙH₂ₙ belongs to the alkenes.
items.random_wrong: C₅H₁₂O — it has 12 hydrogen atoms

items.q: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. What is the separation based on?
items.correct: Differences in the boiling points of the molecules
items.misconception: Differences in how fast the molecules react together
items.why: Anything happening in a large industrial tower is assumed to be a chemical change. Fractional distillation is a physical separation. Nothing reacts; the hydrocarbons are sorted by the temperature at which they condense.
items.random_wrong: Differences in the density of the liquid hydrocarbons

items.q: What do the molecules in one fraction of crude oil have in common?
items.correct: They have a similar number of carbon atoms
items.misconception: They are all molecules of exactly the same compound
items.why: Fractions are given single names like petrol and kerosene, and named substances usually mean one compound. A fraction is still a mixture. What its molecules share is a similar number of carbon atoms, so they boil over a narrow range.
items.random_wrong: They all contain the same number of hydrogen atoms

items.q: How does fractional distillation separate the hydrocarbons in crude oil?
items.correct: The oil is evaporated, then each fraction condenses at a different temperature
items.misconception: The oil is melted, then each fraction freezes out at a different temperature
items.why: Melting and freezing are the pair of changes students meet first, and any temperature-based separation is mapped onto them. Crude oil is already a liquid. It is evaporated, and the fractions are recovered by condensing the vapour back to liquid.
items.random_wrong: The oil is filtered, and the larger molecules are held by a fine mesh

items.q: Why are the fractions containing the largest molecules collected near the bottom of the column?
items.correct: They have the highest boiling points, so they condense first
items.misconception: The bottom of the fractionating column is the coolest part of it
items.why: 'Heat rises' is a genuine and useful idea about convection, applied here to a column that is deliberately cooled towards the top. The vapour is fed in hot at the bottom and cools as it rises, so the top is coolest. That gradient is what sorts the fractions.
items.random_wrong: They are the densest, so they sink down to the bottom

items.q: What are the fractions from crude oil processed to produce?
items.correct: Fuels, and feedstock for the petrochemical industry
items.misconception: Fuels only, because every fraction is burned as a fuel
items.why: Fuels are the use of crude oil that students meet at home and in the news, so it eclipses the feedstock role. Fuels are only half of it. Fractions are also fed into the petrochemical industry to make solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
items.random_wrong: Fuels only, since feedstock is another word for fuel

items.q: Which of these is a fuel produced from crude oil?
items.correct: Kerosene, an aircraft fuel
items.misconception: Bioethanol, from fermentation
items.why: They are liquid fuels used in engines, so they are filed alongside petrol and diesel without asking where they come from. Bio- fuels are made from crops by fermentation or from plant oils. They are not obtained from crude oil at all.
items.random_wrong: Charcoal, made by heating wood

items.q: Which of these are produced by the petrochemical industry?
items.correct: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents
items.misconception: Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene and fuel oil
items.why: 'Petro-' is read as petrol, so the industry is assumed to be the one that makes it. The fuels are listed separately in the specification. The petrochemical industry uses fractions as feedstock to make materials, not fuels.
items.random_wrong: Limestone, cement, sand and glass items

items.q: Why is there such a vast array of natural and synthetic carbon compounds?
items.correct: Carbon atoms can form families of similar compounds
items.misconception: Carbon has far more isotopes than any other element does
items.why: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are well known, so isotopes are the first special thing about carbon that comes to mind. Isotopes differ only in neutrons and behave identically chemically. The variety comes from carbon atoms bonding to each other in families of similar compounds.
items.random_wrong: Carbon atoms bond ionically to form long chains

items.q: Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules. Which set of properties is this?
items.correct: Boiling point, viscosity and flammability
items.misconception: Boiling point, solubility and conductivity
items.why: Any list of properties feels equally plausible when the specific three have not been committed to memory. The specification limits the trends to boiling point, viscosity and flammability. Hydrocarbons do not conduct electricity at all.
items.random_wrong: Colour, density and electrical conductivity

items.q: How do the properties of hydrocarbons change as the molecules get larger?
items.correct: Boiling point up, viscosity up, flammability down
items.misconception: Boiling point down, viscosity up, flammability down
items.why: Petrol, which evaporates readily, is the most familiar fraction, and 'light' fuels are assumed to be the ones that boil at higher temperatures. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling point rises with molecular size.
items.random_wrong: Boiling point rises, viscosity down, flammability up

items.q: How does the boiling point of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?
items.correct: It increases, as larger molecules attract each other more strongly
items.misconception: It decreases, as larger molecules are heavier and move slower
items.why: Petrol, which evaporates readily, is the most familiar fraction, and 'light' fuels are assumed to be the ones that boil at higher temperatures. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling point rises with molecular size.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, since size only affects density

items.q: How does the viscosity of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?
items.correct: It increases, so the liquid flows less easily
items.misconception: It increases, so the liquid catches fire faster
items.why: Viscosity, volatility and flammability are three long words met together, and they blur into a single vague idea of 'how the fuel behaves'. Viscosity is about flow alone. A viscous liquid is thick and pours slowly; it says nothing directly about ignition.
items.random_wrong: It decreases, so the liquid flows freely

items.q: How does the flammability of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?
items.correct: It decreases, so it is harder to ignite
items.misconception: It increases, as there is more carbon to burn
items.why: More fuel per molecule sounds like more burning, and energy released is confused with ease of ignition. Flammability is about how easily the fuel ignites. Large molecules are hard to vaporise, so they are much harder to light.
items.random_wrong: It increases, so it is easier to set alight

items.q: Liquefied petroleum gases are used in portable camping stoves. Which property makes them suitable?
items.correct: They are highly flammable and ignite very easily
items.misconception: They have high boiling points and do not evaporate
items.why: Safety is associated with something that will not evaporate, so a high boiling point is assumed to be desirable. A stove needs a fuel that vaporises and ignites easily. Small molecules with low boiling points are exactly what is wanted.
items.random_wrong: They are very viscous and pour out slowly and safely

items.q: What happens when a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water form, and heat energy is released
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen form, and energy is taken in
items.why: The hydrogen has to go somewhere, and coming out unchanged as an element is the simplest fate to imagine. The hydrogen combines with oxygen and leaves as water. Nothing escapes as hydrogen gas during combustion.
items.random_wrong: Carbon monoxide and water form, and energy is released

items.q: During the combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, what happens to the carbon and the hydrogen?
items.correct: Both are oxidised, because both gain oxygen
items.misconception: Only the carbon is oxidised, not the hydrogen
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the product students name first, so carbon gets the attention and water is treated as a by-product. Water is an oxide of hydrogen. Both elements in the fuel gain oxygen, and both contribute to the energy released.
items.random_wrong: Both are reduced, because both lose oxygen

items.q: Which equation shows the complete combustion of methane, CH₄?
items.correct: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
items.misconception: 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
items.why: Doubling is the move that fixes odd hydrogen counts in some equations, so it is applied without re-checking the other side. Any change must be checked against every element on both sides. Doubling the left alone always unbalances what was previously correct.
items.random_wrong: 2CH₄ + 4O₂ → CO₂ + 4H₂O

items.q: Which equation shows the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈?
items.correct: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
items.misconception: 2C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 6CO₂ + 8H₂O
items.why: Doubling is the move that fixes odd hydrogen counts in some equations, so it is applied without re-checking the other side. Any change must be checked against every element on both sides. Doubling the left alone always unbalances what was previously correct.
items.random_wrong: 2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O

items.q: Ethane has the formula C₂H₆. Which equation shows its complete combustion?
items.correct: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
items.misconception: C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
items.why: Writing the correct formulae feels like the hard chemistry, so balancing is treated as tidying up. Atoms are not created or destroyed. CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O has four hydrogens on the left and two on the right, so it is wrong.
items.random_wrong: C₂H₆ + O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

items.q: What happens to hydrocarbon molecules during cracking?
items.correct: They are broken down into smaller, more useful molecules
items.misconception: They are separated from one another without being changed
items.why: Cracking is met immediately after fractional distillation and both are described as ways of processing fractions. Distillation separates molecules unchanged; cracking breaks covalent bonds and makes molecules that were not present before.
items.random_wrong: They are joined together to make much larger molecules

items.q: Why are the fractions with the largest molecules cracked?
items.correct: There is a high demand for fuels with small molecules
items.misconception: Fuels made of large molecules are in much higher demand
items.why: Large fractions come out of the column in large quantities, and abundance is confused with demand. Supply of long-chain fractions exceeds demand, while short-chain fuels such as petrol are in short supply. Cracking converts one into the other.
items.random_wrong: It is the only way to remove the sulfur from these fuels

items.q: Which two methods of cracking does the specification name?
items.correct: Catalytic cracking and steam cracking
items.misconception: Catalytic cracking and fractional cracking
items.why: Fractional distillation and electrolysis are the process names most recently learned, so they are borrowed to fill the gap. The specification names catalytic cracking and steam cracking. Neither electrolysis nor distillation is involved.
items.random_wrong: Steam cracking and electrolytic cracking

items.q: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?
items.correct: Hydrocarbons are vaporised and passed over a hot catalyst
items.misconception: Hydrocarbons are vaporised and mixed with steam only
items.why: Steam is associated with boiling water at 100 °C, which sets an expectation of moderate conditions. Steam cracking uses no catalyst and a very high temperature – far hotter than boiling water. The steam simply dilutes the hydrocarbon.
items.random_wrong: Hydrocarbons are cooled and poured over a cold catalyst

items.q: What conditions are used for steam cracking?
items.correct: The vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature
items.misconception: The vapour is mixed with steam and then passed over a hot catalyst bed
items.why: Steam is associated with boiling water at 100 °C, which sets an expectation of moderate conditions. Steam cracking uses no catalyst and a very high temperature – far hotter than boiling water. The steam simply dilutes the hydrocarbon.
items.random_wrong: The vapour is mixed with steam and kept at a mild temperature

items.q: The products of cracking include alkanes. What is the other type of hydrocarbon produced?
items.correct: Alkenes, a more reactive hydrocarbon
items.misconception: Only more alkanes, but smaller in size
items.why: The starting material is an alkane, and students expect the products of breaking a molecule up to be the same kind of substance. There are not enough hydrogen atoms to make every product an alkane, so alkenes are formed as well.
items.random_wrong: Alcohols, that contain oxygen as well

items.q: How can you show that a hydrocarbon is an alkene and not an alkane?
items.correct: Add bromine water and shake well
items.misconception: Add bromine water; both will react
items.why: Students remember that alkenes are 'more reactive', which suggests a difference of degree rather than a yes/no test. For this test the alkane gives no reaction and the bromine water stays orange. That is what makes the test useful.
items.random_wrong: Add bromine water; the alkane just reacts slower

items.q: What colour change is seen when bromine water reacts with an alkene?
items.correct: Orange bromine water is decolourised to colourless
items.misconception: Colourless bromine water turns orange in colour
items.why: Positive tests are usually remembered as 'a colour appears', so the direction of this change is reversed. Bromine water starts orange. The alkene reacts with the bromine and removes the colour, so it ends up colourless.
items.random_wrong: Orange bromine water turns a cloudy white colour

items.q: What are alkenes used for?
items.correct: To produce polymers and many other chemicals
items.misconception: Only as fuels for cars, lorries and aeroplanes
items.why: Cracking is introduced as a way of making more fuel, so everything it produces is assumed to be burned. Cracking does supply fuels, but the alkenes are more valuable as feedstock for polymers and other chemicals.
items.random_wrong: Nothing much, as polymers come from alkanes

items.q: Cracking one molecule of C₁₀H₂₂ produces one molecule of C₂H₄. What is the other product?
items.correct: C₈H₁₈, so that all the atoms balance
items.misconception: C₈H₁₆, treating the alkane as CₙH₂ₙ
items.why: CₙH₂ₙ is the tidier pattern and is the formula of the alkenes, which is met alongside it, so the two get swapped. Alkanes are saturated and carry two extra hydrogen atoms at the ends of the chain: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. CₙH₂ₙ belongs to the alkenes.
items.random_wrong: C₁₀H₁₈, since only hydrogen is removed

items.q: Give one reason why cracking is useful.
items.correct: It turns surplus large molecules into fuels
items.misconception: It makes crude oil into a renewable resource
items.why: Cracking is described as making more of the fuels we want, which sounds like making more oil. Cracking cannot create hydrocarbons. It converts a surplus fraction into products in higher demand; crude oil remains finite.
items.random_wrong: It removes all of the carbon dioxide from fuel

items.q: What was crude oil formed from?
items.correct: An ancient biomass of mainly plankton buried in mud.
items.misconception: Crude oil formed from ancient forests of land plants that were buried in swamps.
items.why: This is a real fossil fuel origin story – it is how coal formed – so students who have learned it apply it to every fossil fuel. Coal came from land plants; crude oil came from marine plankton buried in mud. The two fuels have different origins and are worth keeping apart.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is crude oil called a finite resource?
items.correct: Supplies will run out because it is used far faster than it forms.
items.misconception: Finite means that crude oil is only found in a few countries.
items.why: 'Finite' is read as 'limited in where you can get it' rather than 'limited in total amount'. Finite is about total quantity and rate of replacement, not geography. Even if oil were found everywhere it would still be finite.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every carbon compound a hydrocarbon?
items.correct: No. Only compounds of hydrogen and carbon alone are hydrocarbons.
items.misconception: Any compound that contains carbon is a hydrocarbon.
items.why: The 'carbon' half of the word is noticed and the 'hydro' half is treated as decoration. Both elements must be present and no others. Carbon dioxide and ethanol contain carbon but are not hydrocarbons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is crude oil an element, a compound or a mixture?
items.correct: A mixture of a very large number of compounds, mostly hydrocarbons.
items.misconception: Crude oil is a compound made from the elements carbon and hydrogen.
items.why: Students know it is 'made of carbon and hydrogen' and jump to compound, because compounds are what elements make. Each hydrocarbon molecule is a compound, but the oil itself is a mixture of very many different such compounds.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the first four alkanes?
items.correct: Methane, ethane, propane and butane.
items.misconception: The list runs methane, ethane, propane, pentane – or the order of propane and butane is swapped.
items.why: The prefixes meth-, eth-, prop-, but- are not a familiar counting sequence, unlike pent- and hex- which sound like five and six. The first four are methane (1 C), ethane (2 C), propane (3 C) and butane (4 C), in that order. Pentane would be the fifth.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What do the lines in a displayed formula represent?
items.correct: Covalent bonds between pairs of atoms.
items.misconception: The lines show the charges on the atoms, or their relative masses.
items.why: Diagrams in ionic bonding carry charges, and students transfer that habit to covalent drawings. Alkanes are covalent molecules with no charges. Each line is one shared pair of electrons – one covalent bond.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is C₅H₁₀ an alkane?
items.correct: No. An alkane with 5 carbons would be C₅H₁₂.
items.misconception: C₅H₁₀ is an alkane because it is made of carbon and hydrogen.
items.why: Being a hydrocarbon is confused with being an alkane; the general formula is not applied as a test. Every hydrocarbon is not an alkane. Test the formula against CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: with n = 5 that requires 12 hydrogens, not 10.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many covalent bonds are in a molecule of ethane?
items.correct: Seven: one C–C bond and six C–H bonds.
items.misconception: Fourteen: four bonds at each carbon atom and one at each hydrogen atom, added up.
items.why: Students check each atom in turn for a full outer shell, so a bond already counted at one atom is counted again at the atom on the other end. Each bond is shared between two atoms, so adding up the bonds at every atom counts each line twice. Half of fourteen gives the seven lines actually drawn.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is fractional distillation based on?
items.correct: Differences in boiling point between the hydrocarbons.
items.misconception: The heavier fractions simply sink to the bottom of the column because they are denser.
items.why: The heaviest fractions really are collected at the bottom, so density looks like a sufficient explanation. They are collected low down because they condense first, at the highest temperatures. The material moving through the column is vapour, not settling liquid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What do molecules in the same fraction share?
items.correct: A similar number of carbon atoms.
items.misconception: They all contain exactly the same number of hydrogen atoms.
items.why: 'Similar' is upgraded to 'identical', and hydrogen is chosen because it is the larger number in the formula. The specification says a similar number of carbon atoms. The count is not identical, and it is carbon that defines the fraction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does feedstock mean?
items.correct: A raw material fed into a chemical process to make other substances.
items.misconception: Feedstock is another word for fuel.
items.why: The two words appear in the same sentence of the specification and both describe something being 'fed' into a process. A fuel is burned for energy; a feedstock is a starting material converted into new products such as polymers and detergents.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do carbon atoms build so many different compounds?
items.correct: By joining to one another to form families of similar compounds.
items.misconception: Carbon atoms bond ionically to each other to make long chains.
items.why: Ionic bonding is the strong bonding students meet first, so it is offered whenever strong bonds are needed. Carbon atoms share electrons: the bonds in hydrocarbons are covalent. Ionic bonding needs a metal and a non-metal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does viscosity change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
items.correct: It increases, so the liquid flows less easily.
items.misconception: Larger molecules make the liquid runnier, because heavy things pour faster.
items.why: Viscosity is an unfamiliar word and is guessed at from everyday experience of pouring rather than from molecular attraction. Longer molecules tangle and attract each other more, so thick fractions such as heavy fuel oil pour very slowly.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water.
items.misconception: Complete combustion produces carbon monoxide and water.
items.why: Carbon monoxide is memorable because it is dangerous, so it is recalled ahead of the ordinary product. Carbon monoxide is a product of incomplete combustion, when oxygen is short. With plenty of oxygen the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does combustion release or absorb energy?
items.correct: It releases energy.
items.misconception: Combustion takes in energy, because you have to heat the fuel to start it.
items.why: Ignition genuinely needs energy, and that initial input is mistaken for the overall energy change. A small input starts the reaction, but combustion releases far more energy than it takes in. That is why fuels are useful.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does cracking do to a hydrocarbon?
items.correct: It breaks it down into smaller, more useful molecules.
items.misconception: Cracking joins small molecules together to make bigger ones.
items.why: Cracking and polymerisation are both industrial processes involving alkenes, and the direction of change is easily reversed. Cracking breaks large molecules down. It is polymerisation that joins small alkene molecules into long chains.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the purpose of cracking?
items.correct: To convert surplus large molecules into smaller, more useful ones.
items.misconception: Cracking is done to remove sulfur and other impurities from fuels.
items.why: Any extra industrial step is assumed to be a purification, because purifying is the reason students most often meet for processing. Cracking changes the size of the molecules. Removing sulfur is a separate process and is not what cracking is for.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What conditions are used for catalytic cracking?
items.correct: Hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
items.misconception: Catalytic cracking is carried out cold, because a catalyst removes the need for heat.
items.why: Catalysts are taught as a way of speeding up reactions without high temperatures, so heat is assumed to be unnecessary. A catalyst lowers the energy needed but does not remove it. The hydrocarbon must first be vaporised and the catalyst is hot.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the products of cracking?
items.correct: Smaller alkanes and alkenes.
items.misconception: Cracking produces alcohols, because they are the other organic family.
items.why: Alkanes, alkenes and alcohols are three similar-sounding families and the names are interchanged under pressure. Alcohols contain oxygen. Cracking a hydrocarbon with no oxygen present cannot produce them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does bromine water look like after reacting with an alkene?
items.correct: Colourless.
items.misconception: It turns milky white, or goes cloudy.
items.why: Limewater going milky is the best-known positive test at GCSE, and its appearance is transferred to this one. Milky white is the limewater test for carbon dioxide. Bromine water with an alkene simply loses its orange colour.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which hydrocarbons are used to make polymers?
items.correct: Alkenes.
items.misconception: Polymers are made from alkanes.
items.why: Alkanes are the hydrocarbons met most often, so they are offered as the answer to any hydrocarbon question. Alkanes are saturated and unreactive. It is the more reactive alkenes that join together to form polymers.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the petrochemical industry make every industrial chemical?
items.correct: No. It makes materials from crude oil fractions, such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
items.misconception: Anything made by heavy industry – cement, glass, the gases from air – comes from the petrochemical industry.
items.why: 'Chemical industry' is treated as one undivided thing, so the raw material each product actually starts from is never checked. The petrochemical industry starts from crude oil. Cement and glass start from quarried rock, and nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
